clue.text: This kind of fish won't be found in this bay

definitions.text: This kind of fish won't be found in this bay

parts.words: This kind of fish won't be found in this bay
parts.note: the same word names a class of fish from rivers and lakes and a bay on the Isle of Wight, where sea water would kill such fish

explanation.surface: An angler is warned that a certain fish is not to be had in a particular bay.
explanation.walkthrough: Freshwater Bay is on the coast of the Isle of Wight, off southern England; the clue's irony is that a river fish could not live in its salt water.
explanation.definitionFit: Trout, pike and perch are fish of rivers and lakes rather than the sea, and the Isle of Wight bay bears that same name.

clue.text: The game's up — beat it!

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is written from bottom to top

parts.note: golf is the game

explanation.surface: A lookout shouts that the game is up and tells everyone to run.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The game's up' sounds like 'we've been caught', and 'beat it' like 'run away'; really 'up' turns GOLF over and 'beat' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To flog is to beat with a whip or stick.

clue.text: Here's a tip

parts.note: not advice but a pointed end

explanation.surface: Someone about to offer helpful advice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Here's a tip' sounds like advice; the tip is the end point of something.
explanation.definitionFit: The farthest end or point of something, such as a finger or a limb, is its tip.

clue.text: One needs staying power to enjoy it

definitions.text: One needs staying power to enjoy it

parts.words: One needs staying power to enjoy it
parts.note: staying power read as the means to stay overnight as a guest

explanation.surface: Endurance is required to enjoy something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Staying power' means stamina, but here it means the money or right to stay as a paying guest.
explanation.definitionFit: Lodgings for travellers are enjoyed only by those who stay there.

clue.text: They're going up like foreign currency

parts.note: as means like
cents are coins of the US and other foreign currencies

explanation.surface: Prices are rising, as foreign money does.
explanation.walkthrough: Cents are a foreign coin to a British solver, hundredths of a dollar.
explanation.definitionFit: Climbs are movements upward, so they are things going up.

clue.text: One who can be relied upon to show up

definitions.text: One who can be relied upon to show up

parts.words: One who can be relied upon to show up
parts.note: show up read as to unmask or reveal, not to arrive

explanation.surface: A dependable person who always arrives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Show up' seems to mean turn up; here it means to reveal or unmask.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who reveals wrongdoing or lays bare secrets shows things up.

clue.text: It's a trifle when the playwright gets a kick

annotationWithheld.why: It's a trifle when the playwright gets a kick (4): SHAW plus P gives PSHAW, a cry dismissing a trifle, but no clue word clearly gives the P ('kick' does not), so no honest parse can be written
annotationWithheld.clue: It's a trifle when the playwright gets a kick

clue.text: So he could be getting a following as a prophet

indicators.note: following means the next piece comes after the jumbled letters
could be means the letters might form something else, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A man might gain disciples as a prophet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'could be' turns SO HE into HOSE, and 'getting a following' puts A after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Hosea is one of the minor prophets of the Old Testament.

clue.text: Gain one city and rifle another

parts.note: to win is to gain
Chester is a city in north-west England

explanation.surface: Someone captures one city and plunders another.
explanation.walkthrough: WIN plus CHESTER gives another English city, Winchester, which is also a famous American rifle; 'rifle' looks like a verb meaning plunder.
explanation.definitionFit: The Winchester repeating firearm is a classic American gun of the Old West.

clue.text: Ay, there's the rub

parts.note: Hamlet's phrase, where rub means difficulty, read literally as rubbing

explanation.surface: Hamlet's line from his famous soliloquy.
explanation.walkthrough: In Hamlet 'rub' means an obstacle; read literally, rubbing is resistance between surfaces.
explanation.definitionFit: Rubbing between two surfaces is the resistance physicists call by this name.

clue.text: One of those pieces of eight

definitions.text: One of those pieces of eight

parts.words: One of those pieces of eight
parts.note: pieces of eight are pirate coins, but here the pieces are compositions written for eight players

explanation.surface: A pirate holds up one of his Spanish silver coins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pieces of eight' calls up pirate treasure, but read as musical pieces for eight performers it defines the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A composition scored for eight instruments or voices is called by that name, as a quartet is for four.

clue.text: A cap, sir ? No, something to put on a horse

annotationWithheld.why: A cap, sir? No, something to put on a horse (9): CAPARISON is an anagram of A CAP SIR NO, but this 1930s-style clue has no anagram indicator, and every remaining word is fodder or definition, so no word can honestly be named as the signal
annotationWithheld.clue: A cap, sir ? No, something to put on a horse

clue.text: Distributive transactions ?

parts.note: business deals, read also as the handing round of cards to each player

explanation.surface: An economist's term for trades that share goods out.
explanation.walkthrough: Business transactions are dealings; the question mark points to the card-table sense, where dealing hands out the pack.
explanation.definitionFit: Trading activity is called business dealings, and a dealer at cards distributes the pack.

clue.text: Vehicle of instruction

definitions.meaning: a bus or carriage for passengers
a tutor or trainer who instructs pupils or players

explanation.surface: A grand phrase for a teaching aid, as if lessons rode in a carriage.
explanation.definitionFit: A long-distance bus or horse-drawn carriage shares its name with a sports trainer or private tutor.

clue.text: Clean homes for lizards

annotationWithheld.why: Clean homes for lizards (10): CHAMELEONS is an anagram of CLEAN HOMES, but the clue has no anagram indicator ('for' is only a link), so the op has no signalling word

clue.text: With all that money it's odd she's full of anger

indicators.note: the jumbled word holds the next piece within it, as a vessel full of something
odd means strange or out of order, so the letters of the clue word are jumbled

parts.note: she's written out gives the four letters S, H, E, S
ire is anger

explanation.surface: A rich woman, oddly, is in a constant temper despite her fortune.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With all that money' looks like a scene-setting phrase but is the definition; 'odd' jumbles the four letters of she's, and 'full of' wraps them round the word for anger.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman due to inherit a great fortune is described as having all that money.

clue.text: Output of spirits ?

parts.note: spirits as ghosts being put out, not the production of a distillery

explanation.surface: A distillery's production of whisky and gin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Output of spirits' suggests a distillery; here the spirits are evil ones being cast out.
explanation.definitionFit: Driving out demons or evil spirits is the rite performed by a priest.

clue.text: Excursionists of an offensive character

parts.note: trippers who make excursions, read as soldiers making sorties against an enemy

explanation.surface: Rude day-trippers spoil an outing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Offensive' suggests rudeness, but in the military sense it means attacking; an excursion here is a sortie.
explanation.definitionFit: Attackers who make swift incursions into enemy ground, such as commandos or bandits, make military excursions on the offensive.

clue.text: To cut a long story short, for instance

definitions.text: To cut a long story short, for instance

parts.words: To cut a long story short, for instance
parts.note: the phrase is read as an example of summing up briefly

explanation.surface: A speaker hurrying to the end of an anecdote.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase seems like a speaker's aside, but it is offered as an example of the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To summarise or abridge is to give the essence in brief, as when cutting a story short.

clue.text: Rustic dance centre

parts.note: not a village hall but the object a country dance circles round

explanation.surface: A village hall where country folk go dancing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dance centre' sounds like a venue; in a May Day country dance the centre is the tall ribboned pole the dancers circle.
explanation.definitionFit: On May Day, villagers dance round a tall ribboned post on the green, so it stands at the heart of the rustic dance.

clue.text: It is made with 24

parts.note: the entry at 24, a query, is what an investigation is made with

explanation.surface: A cross-reference to another clue in the puzzle.
explanation.walkthrough: 24 across is QUESTION; an investigation consists of asking questions.
explanation.definitionFit: An investigation proceeds by putting queries, so it is made up of them.

clue.text: One might hear a good report of it

definitions.text: One might hear a good report of it

parts.words: One might hear a good report of it
parts.note: a good report is praise, but a report is also a loud bang

explanation.surface: Something that enjoys glowing reviews.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'report' is the bang of a gun, so a good report is a loud shot rather than praise.
explanation.definitionFit: Shots from guns make sharp bangs, which are called reports.

clue.text: Ruth at the gathering

parts.note: the biblical Ruth gathered leftover barley in Boaz's field

explanation.surface: A woman named Ruth attending a party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gathering' looks like a social event; in the Book of Ruth she picks up grain left by reapers.
explanation.definitionFit: One who collects the stalks left after harvest, as Ruth did in Boaz's field.

clue.text: Right thinking may be given the chop

definitions.text: Right thinking may be given the chop

parts.words: Right thinking may be given the chop
parts.note: sound reasoning that can be cut up, as in the old phrase for quibbling argument

explanation.surface: Sensible ideas are likely to be scrapped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chop logic' is an old phrase for arguing over fine points; 'given the chop' looks like being axed.
explanation.definitionFit: Correct reasoning is the subject of the study of valid inference, and pedants are said to chop it.

clue.text: Zest for nothing after the end of the month

indicators.note: after means the piece for nothing comes behind the shortened month
the end of signals that only the closing part of the month's name is kept

parts.note: August is the month
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: Enthusiasm for doing nothing once the month is over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the end of' keeps only the closing four letters of the month, and 'after' puts the ring-shaped letter for nothing behind them; 'Zest for nothing' reads as idle enthusiasm.
explanation.definitionFit: Keen relish or enthusiasm is the same thing as zest.

clue.text: Without it, no doubt

parts.note: beyond a query means certainly; without a query there is no doubt

explanation.surface: Something whose absence settles all uncertainty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beyond question' means without doubt, so the clue is defining the thing whose absence leaves no doubt.
explanation.definitionFit: A query raises doubt; take it away and the matter is settled.

clue.text: A Dickens character gets on in Shakespeare

parts.note: Tiny Tim is the crippled boy in A Christmas Carol
taken as written

explanation.surface: A Dickens character appears in a Shakespeare play.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is loose: 'in Shakespeare' stands for a Shakespeare title character, Timon of Athens.
explanation.definitionFit: Timon of Athens is the misanthrope who gives his name to a Shakespeare play.

clue.text: Ben Battle lost his through 21 across

definitions.text: Ben Battle lost his through 21 across

parts.words: Ben Battle lost his through 21 across
parts.note: the soldier in Thomas Hood's comic poem Faithless Nelly Gray whose limbs a cannon-ball took off

explanation.surface: A soldier suffers a loss in battle from gunfire.
explanation.walkthrough: Hood's poem opens: 'Ben Battle was a soldier bold... But a cannon-ball took off his legs.' 21 across is GUNFIRE.
explanation.definitionFit: The soldier in Hood's poem lost his lower limbs to a cannon-ball.

clue.text: One boss is enough to occupy one's mind

annotationWithheld.why: One boss is enough to occupy one's mind (9): OBSESSION is an anagram of ONE BOSS IS, but the clue has no anagram indicator ('enough' links to the definition), so the op has no signalling word
annotationWithheld.clue: One boss is enough to occupy one's mind

clue.text: State of hair, we hear ?

indicators.note: we hear signals that the word for hair is said out loud

parts.note: a mane is the long hair on a horse or lion

explanation.surface: Someone asks what condition their hair is in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'State of hair' reads as condition; 'State' is the US state and 'we hear' turns MANE into its sound-alike.
explanation.definitionFit: Maine is the north-easternmost of the United States.

clue.text: Amongst other goings-on this is proverbially a must

definitions.text: Amongst other goings-on this is proverbially a must

parts.words: Amongst other goings-on this is proverbially a must
parts.note: the saying that a theatrical performance must go on whatever happens

explanation.surface: A remark that, whatever else happens, one thing must continue.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'the show must go on' makes the performance the one going-on that is compulsory.
explanation.definitionFit: A theatrical performance is, by the old saying, the thing that must go on.

clue.text: Grand? Ah, yes, when arranged in the garden

indicators.note: arranged means set out in a new order, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone approves a grand flower arrangement in the garden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arranged' shuffles GRAND, AH and YES; the definition is loose, naming the shrubs by where they grow.
explanation.definitionFit: These are flowering shrubs with big round heads of blossom, a common garden plant.
